analysis.one_liner: Requires all health plans to cover HIV-prevention drugs free of charge and funds PrEP for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a single senator with no cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, TRICARE, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, and the Indian Health Service to cover HIV-prevention medication (PrEP) and its associated testing and follow-up with no copays, deductibles, or prior-authorization hurdles. It would also have barred life, disability, and long-term care insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums because someone takes PrEP, created a $60 million-a-year grant program to get PrEP to uninsured people, and funded a CDC public education campaign.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.1 million Americans who could benefit from PrEP but, as of 2016, only 7 percent were getting it — especially Black and Latino people, gay and bisexual men, transgender women, and uninsured people, who faced the largest cost barriers. The drug's list price exceeded $20,000 a year, and the bill's own findings show PrEP users were disproportionately White while those eligible were disproportionately Black [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of HIV, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Requires private insurance plans to cover FDA-approved HIV-prevention drugs plus lab tests and follow-up care with no cost-sharing and no preauthorization requirement [S2] [S3].

Extends the same no-cost coverage to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, the VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service, closing gaps the existing preventive-services mandate left open [S2] [S3].
Provides federal grants so uninsured people can get PrEP regardless of insurance status, prioritizing communities where PrEP is underused [S2] [S3].
Prohibits life, disability, and long-term care insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums because a customer takes HIV-prevention medication [S2] [S3].

Creates a CDC public education campaign designed with community organizations to raise awareness of PrEP and counter stigma, and directs HHS to update privacy rules so people can use these benefits on a family plan without other family members being told [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers bear the cost of covering PrEP and its associated services with no cost-sharing, which is spread across premiums; federal taxpayers fund the $60 million-a-year grant program and the education campaign; and life, disability, and long-term care insurers give up the ability to price or deny policies based on PrEP use [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, premium payers, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The coverage mandates push costs into premiums for all plan enrollees, and because the bill requires coverage of FDA-approved drugs without negotiating prices, a brand-name maker could keep charging its roughly $20,000-a-year list price at the time of introduction — the bill itself noted only one branded PrEP was FDA-approved and a cheaper generic was not yet available [S3].

The grant program is authorized at $60 million per year for five years, a real but permanent addition to federal spending, and the education campaign is funded through fiscal year 2026 with no fixed dollar cap [S3].

A blanket ban on pricing life and disability policies based on PrEP use removes underwriting discretion entirely; a good-faith critic could argue insurers should be able to consider any medically relevant fact, though the bill asserts PrEP use carries no additional actuarial risk worth pricing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is large and well-documented: daily PrEP cuts the risk of getting HIV from sex by over 90 percent, yet fewer than one in ten people who could benefit were using it, largely because of cost. The main costs are higher premiums and roughly $60 million a year in federal grants. The bill's biggest design weakness is that it mandates payment for the drug at whatever price the maker charges rather than pairing expanded access with price negotiation, so some of the spending would flow to the manufacturer rather than to patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended in January 2021 [S1] [S4] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the PrEP Access and Coverage Act in the Senate on June 20, 2019 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no further action appears in the legislative record [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year session [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers avoided a new no-cost-sharing coverage mandate with no preauthorization allowed, and life, disability, and long-term care insurers avoided a ban on pricing and denying policies based on PrEP use. No federal grant money was appropriated. The communities at highest risk of HIV, who the bill's own findings showed faced cost barriers to a drug listed above $20,000 a year, gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and was its only sponsor; no other senator cosponsored it [S1] [S4] [S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Lamar Alexander, R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 20, 2019 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out; the legislative record shows no committee action before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions exist; it drew a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, leaving its level of support in both parties unknown [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required private plans to cover PrEP drugs, testing, and follow-up with no cost-sharing and no preauthorization, shifting those costs onto insurers and ultimately premiums. Insurers preferred the status quo, in which the 2019 preventive-services recommendation was narrower and left gaps for Medicare and Medicaid [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Life, disability, and long-term care insurers
industries.note: The bill would have made it unlawful to deny coverage, limit benefits, or raise premiums for anyone taking HIV-prevention medication, removing a pricing lever these underwriters used [S2] [S3].

At introduction, the only FDA-approved PrEP carried a list price above $20,000 a year, and the bill mandated that every insurance program cover it with zero cost-sharing while setting no price limits — locking in the manufacturer as the paid supplier of an expanded customer base. Wider access would have driven volume, with the bill itself noting a generic was expected in late 2020 [S3].
